Charis. p. 138; Diom. p. 326 P. (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 227, 245

1āctīvus: long a (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). From āctus, long by Lachmann’s law (Gell. 9.6.3), as āctiō.

āctīvus1, āctīva, āctīvum

Declension on Wiktionary

The later grammarians’ term: verbum āctīvum, an active verb; genus āctīvum, the active voice (Traupman 245). For the grammarians an āctīvum verb was transitive, against neutra. Quintilian calls it faciendī modus, “the mode of doing” (see below).

Other words

  • faciendī modus — the active voice, “the mode of doing”

    also used · classical · Quint. 9.3.7: et contrā faciendī quae patimur, ut vāpulō

    Quintilian’s name, set against patiendī modus, the passive. The older name; the grammars and the classroom use the later one.

Examples

  • in nātūrā verbōrum est et quae facimus patiendī modō saepe dīcere, ut arbitror, suspicor, et contrā faciendī quae patimur, ut vāpulō

    it is in the nature of verbs often to say what we do in the passive, as arbitror, suspicor, and on the other hand in the active what we suffer, as vāpulōQuint. 9.3.7

  • Cujus generis est? Āctīvī an passīvī? — Āctīvī.

    What voice is it? Active or passive? — Active.Traupman 241

See also voice, passive, transitive.
